# Part 6: Data Architecture

Retrieval quality is bounded by corpus quality, and no prompt fixes a bad corpus. That sentence is the whole argument for this part and it is the sentence that gets nodded at and then ignored, because prompt work is visible and data work is not. The architectural consequence is blunt: **when an AI system underperforms and the data was never assessed, the data is the first suspect and the model is the last.**

---

## 6.1 Data quality as an AI precondition

### The six dimensions

| Dimension | Definition | How it fails an AI system specifically |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Completeness** | The expected values are present | Missing fields are the direct cause of fabrication. A model asked to produce a required field it cannot find produces a plausible one. Missing documents are worse, because retrieval returns the nearest available thing and the answer is confidently wrong with a working citation |
| **Accuracy** | The value corresponds to reality | The system launders bad data into authoritative-sounding prose. A wrong figure in a source becomes a wrong figure in an answer, now carrying a citation and the institutional voice of the assistant |
| **Consistency** | The same fact agrees across systems and records | Contradictory sources produce arbitrary selection. The model picks one, usually the one that ranked highest, and does not report the conflict. **Conflicting sources are worse than missing sources**, because absence is detectable and contradiction is not |
| **Timeliness** | The value is current enough for the decision | Superseded policy retrieved as current. This is the characteristic enterprise retrieval failure and it presents as a correct answer to yesterday's question |
| **Validity** | The value conforms to its defined format and domain | Dates in three formats, currency without a unit, identifiers that do not match their pattern. Downstream parsing fails silently or coerces wrongly, and the model reasons over the coerced value |
| **Uniqueness** | One real thing, one record | Duplicate documents dominate retrieval results, crowding out diversity so that the top five chunks are five copies of one paragraph. Near-duplicates with small differences are worse, because the model treats them as corroboration |

**Decision rule: assess the six dimensions on a sample of the actual corpus before designing the pipeline, because each of them changes either the design or the expected quality ceiling, and most change both.**

Two of these deserve elevation. **Timeliness fails silently and is the dimension most often unmeasured**, because a document that was correct when indexed does not announce that it has been superseded. And **uniqueness is the dimension most underestimated**, because deduplication is treated as hygiene rather than as a retrieval quality intervention, and duplicate crowding is one of the largest single sources of poor retrieval diversity in real corpora.

### Measurement and a quality scorecard

Quality that is not measured per source is not managed. The scorecard is per source system, not per corpus, because remediation is always addressed to an owner.

| Column | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Source** | The system or collection, named at the granularity someone owns |
| **Owner** | A named accountable person. An unowned source cannot be remediated and its quality is therefore fixed |
| **Volume and growth** | Documents and rate, because a source growing faster than it is curated degrades |
| **Score per dimension** | Six numbers, measured, with the sampling method stated |
| **Coverage** | What fraction of the questions in scope this source can answer at all |
| **Freshness lag** | Time from change in the source to availability in the index, measured rather than designed |
| **Known exclusions** | What is deliberately not indexed and why, because an undocumented exclusion becomes an unexplained failure |
| **Remediation** | Fix at source, fix in pipeline or accept with a stated limit. Three options and the third is legitimate |

The measurement methods that work: **validity and uniqueness are computable** directly over the corpus; **completeness is computable** against a declared schema; **consistency is computable** by cross-source comparison on a shared key; **timeliness is computable** if the source carries effective and modification dates and is unmeasurable if it does not; and **accuracy requires sampling with human adjudication** and cannot be automated, which is why it is the dimension most often asserted and least often measured.

**The rule that governs all of it: retrieval quality is bounded by corpus quality.** A retrieval system cannot return a document that is not there, cannot prefer the current version if version is not recorded and cannot exclude what the user may not see if permission is not carried. Every one of those is a data property, not a retrieval algorithm property. **No prompt fixes a bad corpus, and an evaluation that improves after prompt changes on a bad corpus has measured something other than what it intended.**

## 6.2 Data modeling for AI

### Three levels, and why the AI system needs all three

| Level | Answers | Audience | AI-specific content |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Conceptual** | What things exist and how they relate, in business language | Business and legal stakeholders | Establishes whether "document", "matter" and "obligation" mean one thing across the enterprise. Usually they do not, and the discovery is the value |
| **Logical** | Entities, attributes, keys and relationships, technology-independent | Architects | Where the AI-native entities are introduced and where the permission model becomes explicit |
| **Physical** | Tables, indexes, vector stores, object storage, partitions | Engineers | Where chunking, embedding dimensionality, index type and partitioning by tenant get decided |

**Decision rule: if the conceptual model has not been agreed, the physical model is encoding a disagreement, and it will surface as inconsistent answers that look like model failures.**

### The eight entities a transaction system does not have

An enterprise resource planning system models customers, orders and invoices. It does not model any of the following, and each is required for an AI system to be governable rather than merely functional.

| Entity | What it holds | What breaks without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Document** | The logical source artifact, with version, effective date, status, jurisdiction, owner and permission set | Superseded content is retrieved as current, and "which version did it read" is unanswerable |
| **Chunk** | The retrievable unit, with its offsets into the document, its inherited metadata and its own identifier | Citations cannot be resolved back to a location, and re-chunking silently changes what was retrieved |
| **Embedding** | The vector, with its model identifier, dimensionality and generation timestamp | A model upgrade mixes incomparable vectors in one index, which degrades quality with no error anywhere |
| **Run** | One execution, with inputs, configuration, retrieved context, tool calls, output and cost | Nothing about the system is reconstructable. This is the entity teams add last and need first |
| **Evaluation** | A scored judgment about a run or an output, with the rubric version and the grader identity | Quality has no history and regressions are discovered by users |
| **Decision** | The consequential action the system recommended or took, its authority basis and its stakes classification | The record a regulator asks for does not exist |
| **Override** | A human's correction of a system output, with the reason and the corrected value | The most valuable training and evaluation signal in the enterprise is thrown away at the moment it is produced |
| **Evidence** | The specific chunks, values and computations that support a specific claim in the output | Explanation is reconstructed after the fact, which means it is invented after the fact |

Two structural points. **Chunk is a first-class entity, not a derived artifact.** Teams that treat chunks as an ephemeral output of a pipeline discover that they cannot answer which chunk produced a sentence after a reindex, because the identifiers changed. Chunk identifiers must be stable across re-runs where the content is unchanged, and a chunk whose content changes gets a new identifier rather than a mutated record.

And **override is the entity with the highest value-to-effort ratio in this table.** It is free labeled data, produced by the exact population whose judgment the system is trying to approximate, and it is discarded by default because the interface treats an edit as a correction to a draft rather than as an event worth recording.

### System of record, system of engagement, system of intelligence

| | System of record | System of engagement | System of intelligence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Holds** | Authoritative state | The interaction | Inference, retrieval, synthesis and judgment |
| **Truth claim** | It **is** the truth | It reflects the truth | It **proposes** something about the truth |
| **Consistency** | Strong, transactional | Session-scoped | Eventually consistent with both, and often stale |
| **Failure** | Data corruption, which is catastrophic and visible | Poor experience | **A confident wrong proposal, which is neither catastrophic nor visible** |
| **Retention** | Long, regulated | Short | Medium, driven by evaluation and audit needs |
| **May write to** | Itself | The system of record, through controlled paths | **Nothing directly.** It proposes; another system, or a human, commits |

**Decision rule: the system of intelligence never becomes the system of record, and any design where the only place a fact lives is the AI system's own store has misassigned the layer.**

That rule has a practical edge that comes up constantly. An extraction pipeline that pulls obligations out of contracts and stores them in its own database has created a new system of record by accident, with no ownership, no change control, no reconciliation to the contracts it came from and no defined behavior when a contract is amended. The correct design writes extractions back into an owned system with provenance attached, or holds them explicitly as **derived, dated and reproducible** artifacts that are regenerated rather than maintained.

```
  SYSTEM OF RECORD        SYSTEM OF INTELLIGENCE      ENGAGEMENT
  +----------------+      +---------------------+     +---------+
  | contracts      |      | corpus + chunks     |     | chat    |
  | claims         |--+   | embeddings + index  |     | review  |
  | customers      |  |   | runs / evals        |     | queue   |
  | entitlements   |  |   | overrides           |     +---------+
  +----------------+  |   +---------------------+          ^
        ^             |          |      ^   |               |
        |             +--ingest--+      |   +---propose-----+
        |                +metadata+     |                   |
        +----------commit (authorized)--+-------------------+
              (human or authorized service, never the model)
```

---

## 6.3 Metadata as the load-bearing layer

Metadata is not documentation about the data. **In a retrieval system metadata is the mechanism by which retrieval is governed**, because every control that matters at query time is implemented as a predicate over metadata: permission, tenant, jurisdiction, recency, version, sensitivity and source authority. A chunk with excellent text and no metadata is ungovernable and therefore unusable in any regulated context.

### Five categories

| Category | Contains | AI consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Descriptive** | Title, author, subject, keywords, summary | Improves both filtering and hybrid retrieval, and gives the model something to state when it cites |
| **Structural** | Position in document, section path, parent and sibling chunks, page and offset | Enables retrieval at the right granularity, expansion to neighbors and citation to a location a human can verify |
| **Administrative** | Format, size, ingest date, index version, embedding model, retention class | Enables reindex decisions and answers "was this chunk produced by the old pipeline" |
| **Provenance** | Source system, source identifier, extraction method, transformation history, confidence | The substrate of explanation and the only defense against a challenged answer |
| **Governance** | Classification, permission set, jurisdiction, legal hold, owner, effective and expiry dates, supersession | **The set that decides whether a chunk may be returned to this user, now, for this purpose** |

### The nine fields a chunk must carry

| Field | Without it |
| --- | --- |
| **Source document identifier and version** | You cannot tell which version answered, and reindex breaks every citation |
| **Effective date and, where applicable, expiry** | Superseded content is indistinguishable from current content |
| **Jurisdiction or applicability scope** | The wrong country's rule is retrieved for a question whose answer depends on country |
| **Sensitivity classification** | Routing and redaction cannot be enforced, since both are predicates on this field |
| **Owner** | Nobody can approve a correction or answer a question about accuracy |
| **Permission set or the key that resolves to one** | Filtering before similarity is impossible, so the index is a disclosure channel |
| **Supersession pointer** | The system cannot say "this was replaced by that", which is the single most useful thing it can say about a policy document |
| **Structural path** (document, section, subsection, offsets) | Citation degrades to document-level, which a reviewer cannot verify efficiently |
| **Ingest and index provenance** (pipeline version, embedding model, chunker version) | You cannot scope a reindex, and mixed-generation content silently coexists |

**Decision rule: if a governance control cannot be expressed as a predicate over chunk metadata, it cannot be enforced at retrieval time and must be enforced by excluding the content from the index entirely.**

That rule is the practical resolution of most hard cases. Content whose access rules are too dynamic or too complex to express as metadata does not get filtered cleverly; it gets a separate index, or it stays out. Two indexes with clean rules beat one index with a rule engine nobody can audit.

### Supersession, stated plainly

Enterprises do not delete policy. They replace it, and both versions persist because the old one governed conduct during the period it was in force. Three requirements follow.

1. **Both versions are indexed**, because "what was the policy in March" is a legitimate and frequent question.
2. **Currency is a metadata property, not an indexing decision.** The default retrieval filter selects current, and historical retrieval is an explicit mode.
3. **The supersession relationship is recorded on both records**, forward and backward, so that retrieving an old version can announce its own obsolescence rather than relying on the reader to notice a date.

---

## 6.4 Data classification and handling

### A four-tier scheme

Four tiers is the workable number; five is defensible where a regulated category needs its own handling. More than five gets guessed at, and a guessed classification is worse than none, carrying false assurance.

| Tier | Definition | Handling | Model routing consequence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Public** | Released or releasable without harm | No restriction | Any route. Usable in shared examples and cached prefixes |
| **Internal** | Ordinary business information. Harm from disclosure is limited | Access on employment, not on need | Standard managed route with contractual protections. Logging permitted |
| **Confidential** | Disclosure causes material harm: commercial, competitive, contractual or personal | Need to know, access logged, encrypted at rest and in transit | Route determined by the contractual and residency position. **Content logging restricted or disabled.** Redaction on the way in |
| **Restricted** | Disclosure causes severe harm, or the category is legally special | Named individuals, explicit approval, full audit, often technical isolation | Private or isolated deployment route, or **the content does not go to a model at all.** Human review of outputs. No caching across principals |

**Decision rule: classification sets the deployment route before cost or latency, and a design optimized for cost on a route the classification forbids is not a design.**

Three mechanical consequences to implement rather than describe.

| Consequence | Implementation |
| --- | --- |
| **Routing** | The gateway resolves classification from the request or from the retrieved content's metadata and selects the permitted deployment. It is a policy lookup, not a code branch in each application |
| **Logging** | Prompt and response logging is a per-tier setting. The tier that most needs an audit trail is often the tier that most restricts content logging, and the resolution is metadata-only audit records with content held in a segregated store |
| **Caching** | Cache keys are scoped by tenant and by classification. A cache shared across principals is a disclosure channel that no access control review will find, because the access control is correct and the cache is beneath it |

### The reclassification problem

**A synthesis of public documents can be more sensitive than any of its inputs.** Three individually public inputs can combine into a competitive analysis, a pattern of litigation exposure or an inference about an individual that none contains: the **aggregation and inference problem**, the hardest classification issue in AI, since classification schemes inherit and inheritance is exactly wrong here.

Four architectural responses, in order of preference.

1. **Classify the output by purpose, not by inheritance from inputs.** The template, workflow or use case carries a floor classification, so a competitive analysis is confidential regardless of source tiers.
2. **Route by combination.** Certain source combinations trigger a higher tier, as policy at the gateway rather than a judgment by the user.
3. **Human classification at the point of export.** When content leaves the system, a person confirms its tier: the control that actually works, and the one users resist.
4. **Restrict distribution of outputs by default** to the requesting principal, so reclassification is deliberate rather than a consequence of sharing.

**Decision rule: an output's classification is the higher of its inputs' and the one its purpose implies, and purpose usually wins.**

⚠ **Special categories.** Data protection regimes define categories carrying heightened obligations, commonly health, biometric and genetic, alongside sector regimes for financial, health and children's data. The set, obligations and lawful bases vary by jurisdiction and change. **The architectural consequence is fixed and the legal detail is not:** special-category content must be detectable at ingest so it can be tiered; its presence recorded as metadata so routing and logging respond; and a route must keep it inside a defined boundary. Which categories apply, what lawful basis is required and whether a purpose is permitted are for counsel and the privacy function.

---

## 6.5 Information architecture

### Taxonomy, ontology and folksonomy

| | Taxonomy | Ontology | Folksonomy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Structure** | Hierarchy of categories | Typed entities with typed relationships and rules | Flat user-applied tags |
| **Answers** | Where does this belong | How do these things relate, and what follows | What did people call this |
| **Cost** | Moderate to build, ongoing to maintain | High to build, high to maintain, needs a specialist | Near zero |
| **AI use** | Metadata filters, routing, permission scoping, evaluation segmentation | Entity resolution, multi-hop reasoning, constraint checking, graph retrieval | Recall improvement, vocabulary discovery, a signal about what users actually call things |
| **Failure** | Ambiguous or overlapping categories, so classification is inconsistent | Over-modeling. An ontology nobody maintains is worse than none | Synonym sprawl and no reliability |

**Decision rule: build the taxonomy because filters depend on it; harvest the folksonomy because it tells you the vocabulary users bring; and build an ontology only when the questions require traversing relationships rather than retrieving text.**

That last clause is the discriminator. The question "what does the indemnity clause say" is a retrieval question and needs no ontology. The question "which of our contracts have an indemnity obligation to any subsidiary of this counterparty" is a traversal question and retrieval alone will not answer it correctly at any prompt quality, because the join is not in the text.

### Controlled vocabularies

A **controlled vocabulary** is the agreed set of terms for a field, with one preferred term per concept and synonyms mapped to it. Four properties make one useful for an AI system.

1. **Preferred terms and variants both recorded**, so that a query using a variant matches content using the preferred term. This is the cheapest single retrieval improvement available in most enterprises and it is nearly always skipped.
2. **Stable identifiers per concept**, not strings, so a rename does not orphan every tagged record.
3. **Mapped to the enums used in schemas**, so that the tool contract and the metadata vocabulary are the same vocabulary rather than two that drift.
4. **Owned**, with an addition process. An unowned vocabulary is a snapshot of one moment's opinion.

### Findability as a design goal

**Most enterprise search failures are information architecture failures, not search technology failures.** The evidence is consistent and unglamorous: the content is not there; the content is there in five near-identical versions and none is marked current; the content is there but the permission model prevents the searcher seeing it and no message explains why; the content is there but is titled in a vocabulary the searcher does not use; or the content is there and the searcher does not know it exists to look for.

None of those is fixed by a better ranking function, and all of them are fixed by metadata, curation, vocabulary and structure. This matters for AI because **retrieval-augmented generation inherits every one of these failures and hides them.** A search engine that returns nothing tells the user it found nothing. A generative system that retrieves poorly produces a fluent answer from whatever it did retrieve, which converts a visible failure into an invisible one.

**Decision rule: before adding retrieval sophistication, establish that the content exists, is current, is uniquely represented, is titled in the users' vocabulary, is permitted to the asker and is reachable by someone who does not know it is there, because those six conditions cover the five failures above and none of them is a retrieval problem.**

## 6.6 Data lineage

**Lineage** is the recorded answer to "where did this come from and what happened to it on the way here". In an AI system it operates at three levels and most implementations stop after the first.

| Level | Records | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ingest lineage** | Which source system, which identifier, which version, when fetched, by which connector, under which credential | Freshness, reconciliation, the ability to purge everything derived from a source |
| **Transformation lineage** | Extraction method, cleaning steps, chunker and version, embedding model and version, enrichment steps, each with parameters | Scoping a reindex, explaining a quality change, reproducing a past state |
| **Retrieval lineage** | **Which chunk, of which version, of which document, contributed to which sentence of which output, in which run** | Explanation, defense, dispute resolution, evaluation of retrieval independent of generation |

The third is the one that has to be designed in and cannot be added later. It requires that chunk identifiers survive into the model call, that the output be attributable at a granularity finer than the whole response and that the run record persist the retrieved set including candidates that were retrieved and not used.

### What a lineage record must contain to be usable as evidence

| Element | Why evidentiary use requires it |
| --- | --- |
| **A stable identifier for the output** and the specific claim within it | Disputes are about a sentence, not about a session |
| **Source document identifier, version and hash** | Proves which text existed, not merely which document |
| **Chunk identifiers with offsets** | Lets a reviewer open the source at the location and confirm |
| **Retrieval parameters**: query, index version, filters applied, scores and the candidates rejected | Shows the selection was governed, and shows what was available and not chosen |
| **Model identifier, version and configuration** | Ties the behavior to a specific system state |
| **Prompt template version or hash** | Distinguishes an instruction change from a model change |
| **Timestamps** with a trustworthy clock | Ordering, and correspondence to what was current at the time |
| **The acting principal and the delegation chain** | Answers who caused this |
| **Human decisions**: who reviewed, what they saw, what they changed, when | The difference between an assisted decision and an automated one, which is frequently the decisive question |
| **Tamper evidence**: append-only storage, and integrity protection appropriate to the stakes | A mutable record is a claim, not evidence |

**Decision rule: a lineage record is sufficient when a competent reviewer with no access to the current system state can reconstruct why the system said what it said, and insufficient otherwise.**

Two consequences follow directly. **The retrieved set must be persisted, not recomputed.** Re-running a query months later against a changed index and a changed corpus reproduces a different answer, and presenting that as the explanation is not merely useless, it is misleading. And **lineage retention is set by the dispute horizon, not by the engineering horizon.** Contract disputes surface years later. Observability data retained for weeks is retained for the wrong purpose.

```
  INGEST                 TRANSFORM               RETRIEVE / ANSWER
  +----------+  fetch    +-------------+  chunk  +----------------+
  | source   |---------->| doc v3      |-------->| chunk c81      |
  | DMS/1471 |  hash h9  | eff 2026-02 |  v.7    | offs 4120-4880 |
  +----------+           | juris US    |  embed  | emb model m2   |
                         | class conf  |  m2     +----------------+
                         +-------------+                |
                                                        v
        run r55 : query q, filters {tenant, current},  top-k 8
                  used c81, c14 ; rejected c92, c07
                        |
                        v
        answer a12 : sentence 3  <-- c81 (doc v3, offs 4120-4880)
                     sentence 5  <-- c14
        reviewer u77 : edited sentence 5, reason "outdated rate"
```

## 6.7 Analytics readiness

The failure this section prevents is specific and near universal: a system runs for six months, someone asks whether it worked and the answer requires a project because the events needed to answer it were never emitted.

### Operational telemetry versus analytical data

| | Operational telemetry | Analytical data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | Keep it running | Understand whether it works and what it is worth |
| **Grain** | Per request and per span | Per business event and per outcome |
| **Latency** | Seconds | Hours is fine |
| **Retention** | Weeks to months | Years |
| **Schema** | Loosely typed, changes freely | **Contracted and versioned, because history must remain comparable** |
| **Consumer** | On call | Product, finance, risk, the executive sponsor |

**Decision rule: never answer a business question from the observability platform, because its retention is too short, its schema drifts and its access model is built for engineers.**

### The event model

Eight events, emitted with a contract, cover the measurement needs of most AI systems.

| Event | Key fields |
| --- | --- |
| **run_started** | run id, tenant, user, use case, entry point, model, prompt version, classification |
| **retrieval_performed** | run id, query class, filters, candidate count, top score band, sources used |
| **tool_invoked** | run id, tool, outcome class, duration, error class |
| **output_produced** | run id, output type, token counts, latency segments, cost, stop reason |
| **human_reviewed** | run id, reviewer role, decision, time spent, edit distance band |
| **override_recorded** | run id, field or claim, original, corrected, reason code |
| **action_committed** | run id, action type, target system, target record, authority basis, reversibility class |
| **outcome_observed** | run id, business outcome, value, time to outcome, source of the observation |

The last one is the one nobody emits and the only one that answers the question the sponsor asked. **The outcome is usually observed in another system**, days or weeks later, which is precisely why the run identifier must be written into that system's record at the moment of the action rather than merely logged.

Three properties make the event model usable rather than decorative: **the run identifier is present on every event**, so any two events can be joined; **enumerated fields use the controlled vocabulary** rather than free text, so grouping works; and **the schema is versioned with the same compatibility rules as any other contract**, so a change does not invalidate the history it is being compared against.

### The semantic layer

A **semantic layer** is the single definition of each business metric, expressed once and consumed by every report and every query. It matters more for AI systems than for ordinary reporting for two reasons. First, the metrics are contested: "accuracy", "deflection", "time saved" and "adoption" each have four defensible definitions and the difference between them is the difference between a successful program and a canceled one. Second, **an agent that queries the warehouse should query the semantic layer, not the tables**, because a model composing joins over raw tables will produce a defensible-looking number computed differently from the number in the official report, and reconciling two numbers is a worse outcome than having none.

**Decision rule: define each metric once in the semantic layer; expose that layer to both people and agents; and treat any metric an agent computes from raw tables as unofficial by construction.**

### Warehouse and lakehouse

| Pattern | Fit |
| --- | --- |
| **Warehouse** | Modeled, governed, strong access control and excellent for defined metrics. The right home for the event model, the semantic layer and cost attribution |
| **Lake** | Cheap storage of raw and semi-structured content, weak governance by default. The right home for raw documents and for exports awaiting processing, and the wrong home for anything anyone needs to trust |
| **Lakehouse** | Table formats over object storage giving transactional guarantees, schema enforcement and time travel on cheap storage. The pragmatic default where governed tables and raw content must coexist |

The AI-relevant properties are three: **schema enforcement**, so an event contract can be enforced rather than hoped for; **time travel or snapshotting**, so a past state can be reconstructed for reproducibility, which is a lineage requirement expressed in warehouse terms; and **fine-grained access control**, so tenant and classification predicates are enforceable where the data lives rather than in each consumer.

**Decision rule: raw content in object storage with a manifest; contracted events and metrics in the governed warehouse; and nothing that matters in an ungoverned lake.**

### Designing so that "did this work" is answerable

Five artifacts, specified before build, and all five are cheap at design time and expensive afterwards.

1. **The success metric, defined in the semantic layer** with its numerator, denominator and exclusions written down.
2. **The baseline**, measured before deployment. A baseline not captured before launch cannot be recovered, and its absence is the single most common reason AI programs cannot demonstrate value.
3. **The event contract**, including the outcome event and the identifier written into the business system.
4. **The segmentation dimensions**, decided in advance, because aggregate numbers conceal complete failure on one segment and adding a dimension retroactively does not backfill history.
5. **The comparison design**, whether it is a holdout, a phased rollout or a before-and-after with stated confounders acknowledged.

⧉ **The single largest risk in this part: the corpus, the metadata and the baseline are all cheap before launch and effectively unrecoverable afterwards.** Corpus quality assessed after deployment arrives as a list of reasons the system underperforms, with no budget attached. Metadata not captured at ingest cannot be reconstructed for content whose source has since changed. Retrieval lineage not designed in cannot be backfilled for runs that already happened. And a baseline not measured before launch is gone permanently, which means the program's value becomes a matter of assertion at exactly the moment someone asks for evidence. Every one of these is a decision made in the first two weeks whose consequence arrives in month nine.

## 6.8 Data residency and cross-border transfer

⚠ Every claim here is architectural. The legal position varies by jurisdiction, sector, contract and time, and **jurisdictional confirmation requires counsel.**

### Three obligations, not one

Residency, processing location and transfer restriction are habitually discussed as one requirement and are three. **Each has a different architectural answer, and a design can satisfy one and breach another while its documentation says "region" throughout.**

| Obligation | What it constrains | The architectural answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Storage residency** | Where data sits at rest: the object store, the database, the vector index, the backups and the logs | A pinned region per store, plus an inventory of stores that includes the ones nobody calls a store, meaning caches, traces and evaluation sets |
| **Processing residency** | Where computation happens, which includes inference and also embedding, reranking, grading and any model-assisted enrichment | A route per jurisdiction, pinned where the platform supports pinning and evidenced by contract and configuration where it does not |
| **Transfer restriction** | The conditions under which data may cross a border at all, irrespective of where it comes to rest | A named mechanism per flow, and a design in which flows are enumerable rather than emergent |

**The most common error is treating a storage-region setting as an answer to a processing question.** A store configured in a European region says nothing about where the inference, reranking or grading ran, or where the trace was written. The three obligations take three pieces of configuration, usually owned by three teams: only the first reliably appears in a vendor questionnaire, the second moves when a provider adds capacity and the third survives both, since a transfer restriction is not discharged by choosing a region. None answers the sovereignty question: whose law reaches the data rather than where it sits. ⚠ Whether a step is a transfer, and on what basis permitted, is a legal determination varying by jurisdiction, sector and mechanism.

The architectural constraints, which hold regardless of how the legal detail resolves:

| Constraint | Architectural consequence |
| --- | --- |
| **Processing location may be restricted** | Deployment route is decided before cost and latency, and the design must support a route per jurisdiction rather than one global route. A single-region architecture with a plan to "add regions later" is a rewrite later |
| **Transfer mechanisms may be required** | Data flows must be enumerable. You cannot document a transfer you cannot describe, and "the model provider" is not a description of a flow |
| **Sector rules may add requirements** on top of general data protection | Classification must be able to express sector as well as sensitivity, because the handling rule is the intersection of the two |
| **Logs are processing** | Prompt and response logs, caches, evaluation datasets and traces are all copies of the data, in whatever region they are stored. This is the most commonly missed consequence and it is usually missed because logging is designed by a different team than data flows |
| **Retention and deletion obligations may conflict** | A deletion request and a legal hold pull in opposite directions, and the resolution is a legal determination with an architectural precondition: you must be able to find and act on every copy, including embeddings derived from the deleted content |
| **Sub-processors are part of the flow** | The gateway, the vector store, the evaluation tooling and the observability platform all process the data. The inventory is of processing, not of vendors you have a contract with |

### Inference geography is a control with a price

Restricting where inference runs is an architectural control, available on some routes and not others, and one of the few here with a published price. The documented position on Claude 4.6 and later: a **1.1x multiplier on every token category** when US-only inference is specified through `inference_geo`, meaning input, output, cache writes and **cache reads**. The figure is perishable and sits with the others in Appendix I, to be checked before it goes into a model.

Residency is not free, and its price scales with volume rather than with the number of restricted workloads, so a constraint accepted for one regulated use case prices every token that route carries. And **the multiplier applies to cached reads, which is exactly where a caching-heavy design concentrates its volume**. The caching and geography decisions are usually taken by different people in different weeks, and they interact.

**Decision rule: price a residency constraint against cached token volume rather than uncached, because a well-cached design has already moved most of its tokens to the discounted rate and the multiplier follows them there.**

### The subprocessor chain

**The model provider is one link in the chain and the link everyone examines.** The platform or gateway, the vector store, the observability vendor, whatever ships its logs, the evaluation tooling and any tool the provider executes on your behalf are the others: each processes the same content, sits somewhere and has its own onward transfers, which nobody looks at because they are two links from the negotiated contract.

| Link | What it holds or sees | The question usually left unasked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Model provider** | Prompt, retrieved context, output and anything retained | Which region served the inference, and what is retained where and for how long |
| **Provider-executed tools** | Whatever the prompt sends into a tool the provider runs rather than your application, and for a search or fetch tool the query it emits and the content it brings back | Where that execution ran, and whether the tool reached a third party you have no contract with at all. **This is the one link in the chain with no paper**, and 3.3 flags it at the point the tool is enabled, because it is a single configuration line there and a flow here |
| **Platform or gateway** | The same content in transit, plus routing metadata and frequently a copy in its own logs | Whether the gateway's logs sit in the same region as the workload they describe |
| **Vector store** | Chunk text and embeddings, which together are the corpus in another form | Where the index replicates to, including read replicas, backups and disaster-recovery regions |
| **Observability vendor** | Traces, prompts and outputs wherever content capture is enabled, and whatever the log pipeline carries on the way there | Whether content capture is on at all, in which region the traces land, and whether the shipper is a separate processor from the store |
| **Evaluation tooling** | The golden set, which is frequently real regulated content selected for being difficult | Who holds the set, in what jurisdiction, and whether it was ever assessed as a copy rather than as test data |

Each link is named with its location and onward-transfer position, not merely a contract reference. **The chain is a standing register rather than a one-time diligence exercise**, because every link changes without telling you: a vendor adds a region, moves a workload, acquires a subprocessor or changes a default, none of it raising a ticket in your system. Refresh it on a stated cadence and on contract change, under a named owner. ⚠ Which onward transfers require notice, consent or a fresh mechanism is jurisdiction-specific and contract-specific.

### The derived artifact has already crossed

The deletion argument in 5.4 restates for transfer with a sharper edge. **An embedding computed in one jurisdiction from data that may not leave another has already left.** The vector derives from the text and under some conditions supports reconstruction or inference of it, so treating it as a technical artifact rather than a copy has a shelf life. The same reasoning reaches summaries, extracted fields, cached prefixes, evaluation cases, traces that captured content and any fine-tuning corpus.

The architectural consequence does not wait on the legal answer: **every derived artifact carries the residency and transfer attributes of its source**, propagated at creation rather than reconstructed afterwards, because the alternative is a reconciliation across systems whose owners do not know they hold a copy. ⚠ Whether a specific derived artifact is personal data, or its creation a restricted transfer, is for counsel, and the answer is not uniform across jurisdictions.

### Four design properties

Four properties keep the options open, far cheaper to build in than to retrofit.

1. **Region is a first-class attribute** of every record, every index and every route, not a deployment detail.
2. **The data flow inventory is generated from configuration**, not maintained as a document, since a hand-maintained flow diagram is wrong within a quarter.
3. **Deletion is a capability**, exercised and tested, that reaches source, index, embeddings, caches, logs and evaluation sets. **An embedding derived from deleted content is a copy nobody thinks to delete**, the gap most commonly found in review.
4. **Per-jurisdiction routing is a policy lookup at the gateway**, so a change in legal position is a policy change rather than an engineering program.

### The data flow and transfer record

This artifact actually gets requested, by a regulator, a customer's security review, internal audit or the board, and most programs cannot produce it in a usable state on demand. One record per flow, a flow being a movement of content across a boundary rather than an arrow between two systems. **2.8 already requires this record at route selection**, with the paper for each boundary the chosen route crosses. **This is that record kept standing rather than a second one**, and a program that produces two produces two that disagree.

| Element | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Flow identifier and description** | What moves, in business terms. "API call" is not a description of a flow |
| **Data categories and classification** | Including special categories where present, expressed in the tiers the classification scheme already uses |
| **Origin and destination** | Jurisdiction and legal entity, not only cloud region, because the entity determines whose law reaches the data |
| **Purpose** | Why the flow exists, in a sentence the business owner would recognize as their own |
| **Mechanism relied on** | The named transfer mechanism, its date and the assessment supporting it ⚠ |
| **Processors and subprocessors on the path** | Cross-referenced to the standing register rather than duplicated, so one update propagates |
| **Derived artifacts produced** | Indexes, embeddings, caches, logs and evaluation sets, each with its own location |
| **Retention and deletion** | Where each copy is retained, for how long and by which mechanism it is removed |

**Ownership and refresh decide whether the record is real. Accountable: the privacy function. Consulted: the architect.** One side knows the obligation and the other the system, and neither produces it alone, but 4.7 requires exactly one Accountable per artifact and 4.18's own test treats a row answerable with a team name rather than a person as a finding, so joint ownership of this record is a defect wearing the clothes of collaboration. **The privacy function is accountable because the record's purpose is discharging an obligation, and it is the side that answers for the obligation when the record is wrong.** 2.8's lens block names the same record at the moment the delivery route is chosen; it is one record kept standing, not two, and this is the site that specifies it in full. It is refreshed on a stated cadence, on any change of route, region, model provider or subprocessor, and before any filing or attestation relying on it. **Generate it from configuration wherever configuration exists**, design property 2 as a deliverable, since otherwise its wrongness is discovered by the auditor rather than the maintainer.

⚠ **The legal determinations in this section are jurisdiction-specific and they move.** Whether a destination is adequate, which transfer mechanism is available, what assessment must accompany it, whether a sector rule displaces the general position and whether a given step is a transfer at all are questions for counsel in each jurisdiction, and the answers have changed repeatedly within the operating life of such systems. **The architectural requirement is stable and the legal position is not**: the region attribute, the generated flow inventory, the tested deletion capability and the policy-lookup route absorb a change in the legal position as a configuration change rather than a rebuild.

---

## Data Architecture: the one-page version

1. **Retrieval quality is bounded by corpus quality.** Assess the six dimensions on the real corpus before designing anything: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness. Timeliness and uniqueness fail silently. Missing data causes fabrication. Contradiction is worse than absence. Score per source with a named owner, because remediation is addressed to a person.
2. **Model three levels and add the eight entities transaction systems lack:** document, chunk, embedding, run, evaluation, decision, override, evidence. Chunks are first-class with stable identifiers. Embeddings carry their model version. The system of intelligence proposes; something else commits.
3. **Metadata is what makes retrieval governable.** Nine fields per chunk: document and version, effective and expiry dates, jurisdiction, sensitivity, owner, permission set, supersession, structural path, ingest provenance. If a control cannot be a predicate over metadata, enforce it by excluding the content. Index both current and superseded, and filter on currency.
4. **Four tiers, and classification picks the route before cost or latency.** Logging, caching and routing are all per-tier settings. Synthesis reclassifies upward, purpose sets a floor and human confirmation at export is the control that works. Special categories need detection at ingest, metadata recording and a bounded route; the legal detail is for counsel.
5. **Taxonomy for filters, folksonomy for vocabulary, ontology only for traversal questions.** Controlled vocabularies with preferred terms, variants, stable identifiers and an owner. Most enterprise search failures are information architecture failures, and generative retrieval hides them behind fluent prose.
6. **Lineage at three levels, and the third is the one that must be designed in.** Retrieval lineage ties a sentence to a chunk of a version of a document within a run. Persist the retrieved set including rejected candidates. Retention follows the dispute horizon, not the engineering horizon. Evidence needs identity, versions, offsets, parameters, principals, human decisions and tamper evidence.
7. **Analytics readiness is a design-time decision.** Contracted events with the run identifier on every one; an outcome event joined through an identifier written into the business system; a semantic layer that both people and agents query; a governed warehouse rather than an ungoverned lake; and a baseline captured before launch. **Corpus, metadata and baseline are all cheap now and unrecoverable later**, which is the whole argument of this part compressed into one line.
8. **Residency, processing location and transfer are three obligations, not one.** Storage residency is where data sits at rest, processing residency is where computation happens including inference, and transfer restriction is whether the data may cross at all; a design can satisfy one and breach another, and the common error is offering a storage-region setting as the answer to a processing question. Region is an attribute of every record, index and route rather than a deployment detail. The flow inventory is generated from configuration, because a hand-maintained one is wrong within a quarter. Deletion is a tested capability reaching embeddings, caches, logs and evaluation sets, since an embedding computed in one jurisdiction from data that may not leave another has already left. Per-jurisdiction routing is a policy lookup at the gateway, restricting inference geography carries a price multiplier that falls on cached reads too, and the subprocessor chain is a standing register rather than a one-time diligence exercise. ⚠ Adequacy and the available transfer mechanism are counsel's determinations and they move.
